newsitem.title: USA: Punitive damages issue troubles tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: Punitive damages issue troubles tobacco talks.

text.p: Tobacco settlement talks appeared close to collapse again on Tuesday over the issues of regulation by the Food and Drug Administration and punitive damages.
Sources close to the talks said that while progress had previously been made, the industry was now making the two issues contingent on each other.

State attorneys general were waiting Tuesday afternoon for key negotiator Mike Moore, attorney general of Mississippi, to return from a meeting with industry representatives. Several attorneys general said they were willing to walk away from the talks if the issues were not resolved this week.

Talks between tobacco industry representatives and state attorneys general who are suing the industry to recoup the costs of treating diseases allegedly caused by smoking have been going on since early April.
"Enough is enough. There's only so long you can beat a dead horse," said Washington state Attorney General Christine Gregoire.

The attorneys general had hoped to have a settlement proposal to the White House this week, but the mood had grown more pessimistic by Tuesday afternoon. One of the options they had considered was giving the White House an incomplete proposal leaving certain issues like punitive damages unresolved.

The tobacco industry wants protection from punitive damages, which are awarded to punish and deter unwanted behaviour. Some industry representatives are also concerned about language that gives the FDA authority to regulate nicotine as a drug.

Separately, Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey said negotiations between the tobacco industry and attorneys general should be slowed to allow time for the health industry to comment on any proposed deals.

"It's time for this industry to wake up," Humphrey said. "We are going to make sure that when they do wake up, that it's done in the right fashion that we don't have to wake them up again 40 years from now."
Several of the attorneys general involved in the negotiations were critical of Humphrey. Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods called Humphrey "a Johnny one-note."
"We like him, he's our friend, but he's a prohibitionist," Woods said.
The White House on Tuesday refused to help resolve issues delaying a tobacco settlement, saying it was up to the parties to reach a deal in their multibillion-dollar legal battle.

"Broadly stating, they know exactly what our position is on fundamental issues related to protecting kids from tobacco use. I don't think there's any question that they know that they've got to meet that test," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

In return for some protections from lawsuits, the cigarette companies would sharply curtail advertising and stop using cartoon characters, pay penalties if youth smoking is not reduced over certain periods, and pay for programmes to encourage smokers to quit.

Sources said Monday that some negotiators hoped to have a proposed settlement to the White House as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday. But McCurry said the parties still seemed at odds on "issues related to liability and damage payments."
"We can't resolve those issues for them," McCurry said. "We can't render any kind of final verdict on a settlement until we see it."

Deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey, who is perhaps President Clinton's closest aide, has been monitoring the tobacco talks. Two key negotiators, Mississippi's Moore and plaintiffs lawyer Dick Scruggs, met with White House staff Monday afternoon to provide an update on progress.
